title: News Before Breakfast
premise: Read both of the town's newspapers before breakfast. Learn to tell a news story from an ad. Keep one useful clipping.

opening.text:
JAUNT: NEWS BEFORE BREAKFAST. It is sunrise on 1 July 1835. Chicago has two newspapers this summer. They each come out once a week, and one of them is only three weeks old. A dangerous sickness called cholera has been in the state. Everyone wants to know how close it is. But the papers also want to sell you things. Learning to tell news from ads is the most useful thing a newcomer can do.

Choose your question. Ride from the Sauganash to both newspaper offices. Decide which parts tell the news and which parts sell things. Then carry one clipping to breakfast at the Tremont House.

stops.text: Start at the Sauganash. Juliette Kinzie remembered it as a white two-story house with bright blue shutters. In June the paper said it was fixed up and neatly furnished. Both papers are printed a short ride east along the river. Before the town had a paper, news came with the mail. The mail was often late. Somebody would stand on a box and read it out loud. Now you can read it yourself.
stops.narrative: Choose the question you want the papers to answer.

choices.label: Is the cholera near?
choices.consequence: You will read to find news about the sickness.

choices.label: What is new in town today?
choices.consequence: You will read to find anything happening today.

stops.text: John Calhoun printed the Chicago Democrat at this corner starting in 1833. Now it is printed over a hardware store on South Water Street. The paper from 24 June gathers news about the sickness from other towns. It says it could not check one rumor. And it says Chicago is very healthy.
stops.narrative: Is this news, or an ad?

choices.label: Call it reporting
choices.consequence: You put it with the news.

choices.label: Call it an advertisement
choices.consequence: You put it with the ads.

stops.text: Near the drawbridge is the other paper, the Chicago American. It is only three weeks old. Its paper from 27 June has a notice for a medicine called Cholera Elixir. A druggist named Frederick Thomas sells it. The notice says it will surely stop the sickness and cure it. The notice is dated 24 June. That is the same day the Democrat printed its news.
stops.narrative: Is this news, or an ad?

choices.label: Call it reporting
choices.consequence: You put it with the news.

choices.label: Call it an advertisement
choices.consequence: You put it with the ads.

stops.text: Have breakfast at the Tremont House, a wooden hotel from 1833 at Lake and Dearborn Streets. Ira Couch has run it since 1834. Later, in 1850, a new brick Tremont House was built. People thought it was so huge and silly that they called it Couch's Folly. The Democrat says a new auction house is opening on South Water Street. Its first sale is on the 1st of July. That is today!
stops.narrative: Choose one clipping to take with you.

choices.label: Clip the Democrat's cholera paragraph
choices.consequence: The Democrat's news about the sickness goes in your pocket.

choices.label: Clip the Cholera Elixir notice
choices.consequence: The medicine ad goes in your pocket.

choices.label: Clip the auction notice
choices.consequence: The auction notice goes in your pocket.

legs.note: East from the forks along the south bank to the Clark Street corner.
legs.story: Ride east with your question in mind.

legs.note: A block east along South Water Street, toward the Dearborn Street drawbridge.
From near the drawbridge, a block south to the corner of Lake and Dearborn.

endings.text: You asked if the sickness was near. You bring back a news report, not a promise. It has news from other towns, a rumor that could not be checked, and the editor saying Chicago is healthy.
You asked what was new today. You bring back a sale. A new auction room has its first sale on South Water Street, this very morning. The notice does not say what will be sold.
One of the two notices fooled you. That is worth knowing too. The Democrat said which papers its news came from. The medicine ad was signed and sold by the druggist. Read them again over breakfast.
You kept the ad. It promises a sure cure, but a promise is all it is. The seller wrote it, not a news editor. That is a useful thing to know.
You compared two papers before breakfast, and you have one clipping in your pocket. You learned this morning's lesson. A news report says where its news came from. An ad says who is selling.

keepsake.title: A Useful Clipping
keepsake.text: A made-up clipping from a morning's reading of Chicago's two weekly newspapers, kept for what it taught you.

evidence.text: Kinzie describes the Sauganash in 1831 as a white two-storey building with bright-blue wooden shutters.
evidence.locator: Chapter XVII, Chicago in 1831; description of Mark Beaubien’s newly completed house.

evidence.text: The Chicago Democrat reported that the Sauganash had been repaired, fitted up and furnished with neatness.
evidence.locator: 10 June 1835 (Vol. II No. 8), p. 2, col. 5, the paragraph on the town’s public houses (extracted claim chicago_democrat_1835_06_10#c001).

evidence.text: In June 1835 Chicago had two weekly papers: the Democrat, published every Wednesday, and the American, established by T. O. Davis on 8 June 1835 and published on Saturday mornings.
evidence.locator: Democrat, 20 May 1835 (Vol. II No. 5), p. 4, col. 6, the colophon ('Is published every W[ednesday]', transcription lines 4177–4180); Andreas vol. 1, scan p. 767, the Chicago American’s establishment.

evidence.text: The Democrat’s first issue, 26 November 1833, gives its office as the building on the corner of South Water and Clark streets; John Calhoun printed it there.
evidence.locator: 26 Nov 1833 (Vol. I No. 1), the imprint; Andreas vol. 1, the press chapter on Calhoun’s office.

evidence.text: By 20 May 1835 the Democrat’s colophon gives the office as over Messrs. Jones & King’s hardware store, in South Water Street, so the corner is a former office on the scene date.
evidence.locator: 20 May 1835 (Vol. II No. 5), p. 4, col. 6, the colophon (transcription lines 4177–4180). Transcription-mediated reading.

evidence.text: Under the heading CHOLERA the Democrat lays out rumours of the disease in the state: a Springfield paper on the state of health there, the Alton Spectator’s count of about twenty deaths in three weeks with most cases recovering, no mention in the Galenian, and an Ottawa rumour it could not trace. It calls Chicago uncommonly healthy and promises to print the facts if the disease appears.
evidence.locator: 24 June 1835 (Vol. II No. 10), p. 2, col. 5, the paragraph headed ‘CHOLERA.’ (transcription lines 1481–1505; extracted claim chicago_democrat_1835_06_24#c003). Transcription-mediated reading.

evidence.text: The Chicago American’s office was on Water Street near the drawbridge; this project places it on the south side of South Water Street just east of Dearborn, by the south landing of the Dearborn Street bridge.
evidence.reasoning: Andreas gives a street and a landmark, not a lot. The structure record’s inferred position reads the drawbridge as the 1834 Dearborn Street bridge, so the stop says ‘near the drawbridge’ and claims no front door.

evidence.text: The American of 27 June 1835 carries an advertisement headed ‘The Cholera El[ixir]’, offering the Fire King’s Specific as a certain preventive and cure of the asphyxiated cholera, signed by Frederick Thomas, druggist, Water Street, and dated Chicago, 24 June 1835.
evidence.locator: 27 June 1835 (Vol. I No. 4), p. 3, col. 5 (transcription lines 362–365; extracted claim chicago_american_1835_06_27#c011). Transcription-mediated reading: the signature prints ‘FREDERICK THO[…]’, completed from the same druggist’s 20 June notice; the column is crowded and partly illegible.

evidence.text: Alanson Sweet built the first Tremont House, a frame building, in 1833 on the north-west corner of Lake and Dearborn streets. Ira Couch took the house in 1834, and Andreas names the Couch brothers among its keepers before it burned on 27 October 1839.
evidence.locator: Andreas vol. 1, printed p. 635, the hotel chapter (builder, corner, proprietors, the 1839 fire); the Chicago Tribune letter of 2 February 1874 transcribed on chicagology_prefire021, for Ira Couch taking the house in 1834. The structure record tremont_house_1 carries both readings.

evidence.text: A notice headed ‘[Auction an]d Commission House’ announces a store taken on South Water Street for auction and commission business, its first public sale to be held ‘the 1st day of July’, which is the scene date.
evidence.locator: 24 June 1835 (Vol. II No. 10), p. 3, col. 3 (transcription lines 2540–2559, interleaved; extracted claim chicago_democrat_1835_06_24#c008). Transcription-mediated reading; the auctioneer’s surname reads MONTGOMERY and his initials are lost. The American’s 27 June copy of the notice is ambiguous between the first and the last day of July, so only the Democrat’s reading is used.

evidence.text: When the mail came, 'often irregular and long delayed', the town gathered at the post office, where 'some one with a good voice would mount a dry goods box' and read the news from Washington and New York; 'If politics ran high, two dry-goods boxes and two readers of opposite parties would be utilized.'
evidence.locator: p. 99-100, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 13378-13395 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: In the early 1830s Alanson Sweet opened a saloon and boarding house at the north-west corner of Lake and Dearborn, 'the nucleus of the present Tremont House'; its brick successor of 1850 was thought 'absurdly large', and people called it Couch's Folly.
evidence.locator: p. 561, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 98839-98872 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: The four places are exterior stops in the 1 July 1835 scene. The Democrat’s corner is visited as its former office, the American’s office is placed near the drawbridge, and no interior, front door, keeper on the morning or newsroom is claimed.
evidence.reasoning: Uses the existing structure records’ scene-date phases and positions, all of which are inferred. The Democrat’s structure keeps its name but has lost the press by May 1835, so the stop speaks of where the paper was printed, not of a press at work on the morning.

evidence.text: The visitor’s morning, lodging at the Sauganash, the question, the ride on horseback (the recommended mode), the sorting of report from advertisement, breakfast at the Tremont, the choice of clipping, the endings, the timing inputs and the A Useful Clipping keepsake are invented connective narrative, not historical events.
